analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to clearly disclose interest rates, fees, and account terms to depositors.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by voice vote on October 22, 1990 with 103 cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Truth in Savings Act would have required banks, savings institutions, and credit unions to tell customers the true annual percentage yield on deposit accounts, disclose every fee and penalty in a plain-language schedule, mail 30 days' notice before unfavorable account changes, and stop advertising accounts as 'free' when hidden fees or minimum-balance requirements apply. The House passed it without objection near the end of the 101st Congress, but the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary savers and checking-account customers, who could compare accounts across banks on the same terms, see every fee before opening an account, and get advance notice before a bank raises fees or cuts their yield.

how_it_helps.text: Ads citing an interest rate must state the annual percentage yield, all minimum-balance and time requirements, and any fees that could reduce the yield, so advertised rates can be compared honestly [S2][S4].

Each institution must maintain a plain-language schedule of all fees, charges, penalties, and rate terms, provide it to new customers before opening an account, mail it to existing account holders, and give 30 days' notice of changes that would reduce yields or raise costs [S2][S4].
Banks may not advertise an account as 'free' or 'no-cost' if fees, minimum balances, or transaction limits apply, and no ad may be inaccurate or misleading [S2][S4].
Customers who are misled can recover actual damages plus $100 to $1,000 per individual case, with court fees and attorneys' fees paid by a noncomplying institution [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, savings and loan institutions, and credit unions, which must build and mail disclosure schedules, change their advertising, pay the Fed's compliance costs, and face civil liability for violations — costs that could partly be passed back to customers in fees or lower yields.

drawbacks.text: Compliance falls on every depository institution, including small banks and credit unions, which must produce and mail plain-language fee schedules and rework advertising; Congress acknowledged the burden by letting the Fed exempt broadcast and outdoor ads where full disclosure would be 'unnecessarily burdensome' [S2][S4].

Enforcement is narrower than consumer advocates would like: a one-year statute of limitations, a bona fide error defense, class-action recovery capped at the lesser of $500,000 or 1 percent of the institution's net worth, and no liability at all if the bank corrects the error and makes the customer whole within 60 days [S4].
Disclosure rules add paperwork that smaller institutions argued would raise their costs relative to larger competitors, though the bill leaves stronger state disclosure laws in place [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — uniform, honest disclosure so a depositor can actually compare what a bank will pay and charge — is modest per person but applies to nearly everyone with a bank account, and the cost is compliance paperwork rather than a direct transfer. The bill's own enforcement limits (short statute of limitations, capped class damages, a self-correction escape hatch) mean it is more a transparency rule than a teeth-heavy enforcement law. On balance a modest, well-targeted consumer measure.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote with no opposition recorded, but it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Lehman (D-CA) introduced the Truth in Savings Act on January 31, 1989, and it was referred to the House Banking Committee and its Consumer Affairs Subcommittee [S1][S6].
The subcommittee held hearings in May 1989 and forwarded an amended version to the full committee, where it sat for more than a year [S6].

On October 22, 1990, near the end of the Congress, Lehman brought the bill to the House floor under a fast-track procedure requiring no committee report, and the House passed the amended bill by voice vote [S3][S6].

The Senate received the bill on October 23, 1990 and referred it to the Banking Committee on October 27; no hearing, markup, or vote followed before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Depository institutions came out ahead: they avoided mandatory plain-language fee and yield disclosure, the 'free account' advertising ban, and civil liability for misleading disclosures for the remainder of the Congress, while savers kept facing nonstandard, often confusing account terms.

for.name: Rep. Richard H. Lehman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, moved to suspend the rules and pass it on the House floor on October 22, 1990.

for.name: The House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Agreed to the motion to suspend the rules and passed the amended bill by voice vote on October 22, 1990.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the passed House bill on October 23, 1990 and referred it to the full committee on October 27; took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. John Hiler
against.role: House Republican, demanded a second on the suspension motion
against.what_they_did: Demanded a second on the motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill, a routine step that keeps the fast-track floor procedure available.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines — 96 of 257 House Democrats and 7 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, and the House passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded opposition [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill forces honest advertising and plain-language fee disclosure and creates liability for misleading deposit contracts, ending practices like advertising 'free' accounts with hidden fees. Its principal cost to the industry is compliance and the loss of opaque pricing that made cross-shopping hard for customers.

Credit unions face parallel disclosure rules from their own regulator rather than the Fed, so their compliance burden is similar but tailored to their structure. Because they are member-owned cooperatives whose savers are the customers the bill protects, the burden and the benefit land on much the same people.
